opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd want to do is be a bit skeptical of the word "sudden." A lot of what gets described as emergence depends on how we measure. If your metric is exact-match accuracy on a multi-step task, you need every step right, so the score can sit near zero and then shoot up even while the underlying competence improves smoothly. So step one is to look at continuous measures, like the log-likelihood of the correct answer or partial credit, and ask whether there's a real phase transition at all.

Where something does look like a genuine jump, I'd like to see researchers break the task into its component skills and measure each one separately across scale and across training checkpoints. Take multi-digit arithmetic. You can ask whether the model can do single-digit addition, carry correctly, keep track of position, and chain those operations. My guess is you'd often see each of those come online gradually and at different points, and the "emergent" capability appears once the last necessary piece crosses some threshold. That's a very different story from the model suddenly acquiring something new and mysterious.

To do that well, I think we need more of an experimental science mindset. Build controlled synthetic tasks where we know exactly which sub-capabilities are required. Vary the training data so we know when a skill could possibly have been learned. Then use interpretability tools, like probing and causal interventions on internal representations, to check whether the model has actually built the component we think it needs, rather than just inferring it from behavior.

I'd also like to see more attention to the data side. A lot of capabilities may "emerge" because the model has finally seen enough examples of some rare pattern in the training corpus. If we don't know what's in the data, we can't tell whether we're seeing generalization or memorization of something that was effectively there all along.

And finally, there's a practical motivation. If we understand the components, we can predict when a capability will appear, and that matters a great deal for safety and for deployment decisions. Right now we're often surprised after the fact. I'd much rather have a theory, even a partial one, that lets us forecast these transitions and build tests that tell us when a system has acquired a skill we need to worry about, or one we can rely on.

r001.rationale: It proposes measuring each component skill across training checkpoints and says this would reveal when the skills come online.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm somewhat skeptical of the word "emergence" as it's usually used. When people see a capability appear suddenly as you scale a model, there's a temptation to treat that as something almost magical, when in many cases it's an artifact of how we're measuring. If you use an exact-match metric on, say, multi-digit arithmetic, you get a discontinuity, because getting the whole answer right requires getting every digit right. If you look at a smoother metric, like per-token log likelihood or partial credit, you often see a gradual improvement that was there all along. So step one is to be very careful about the measurement, and to ask whether the sudden jump is in the model or in the yardstick.

But let's assume we've done that and there really are cases where a capability seems to come together abruptly. What I'd like to see is a shift from describing these phenomena at the level of benchmark scores to describing them at the level of the sub-skills that have to be in place. Think of something like chain-of-thought reasoning or in-context learning. Those aren't atomic abilities. In-context learning requires that the model can attend back to earlier examples, that it can recognize that those examples share a format, that it can copy or transform the right pieces, and so on. Each of those is a component capability that could in principle be measured separately, and probably has its own learning curve during training.

So my hypothesis, and I think it's a very testable one, is that what looks like a sudden emergence is often a conjunction. You have three or four prerequisite skills that each improve smoothly, and the composite capability only appears when all of them cross some threshold at roughly the same time. Multiply several sigmoids together and you get something that looks very abrupt. If that's right, then the research program is clear: decompose the target capability into candidate components, build diagnostic tasks for each component, and then track them across model scale and, importantly, across training checkpoints, not just across final models of different sizes. We get far too little information from looking only at the endpoints.

The second thing I'd push for is mechanistic work, in the interpretability sense. The induction head story from Anthropic is a nice example. There's a point in training where these two-head circuits form, and in-context learning ability jumps right there. That's the kind of explanation I find satisfying, because it connects the behavioral change to a structural change in the network. I'd like to see that done for many more capabilities, so we can start to build a catalog, if you will, of circuits and the behaviors they support.

And I'll add a third item, which is more about experimental design. We should be doing controlled interventions, not just observational studies. If you believe a capability depends on a certain kind of data, remove that data from the pretraining corpus and see whether the capability still appears. If you believe it depends on a particular circuit, ablate the circuit and see what breaks. We have a tendency in this field to treat large models as natural phenomena to be observed, like astronomers. But we built these systems, and we can run experiments on them, and I think we should take advantage of that much more than we do.

The payoff, from my perspective, is predictability. If we understand the components, we can forecast which capabilities are likely to show up at the next scale, and also which ones won't, and that matters both for engineering and for safety. Surprise is not a property we want in systems we're deploying widely.

r001.rationale: The response proposes measuring component skills across training checkpoints, not only final models, so researchers can track when those skills develop during training.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see us move from observing that a capability suddenly appears to understanding what has to be in place for it to appear. Take a task that seems to exhibit emergence and ask: What are the simpler skills needed to solve it? Can we measure those skills separately as we increase the size of the model or the amount of training?

You could imagine the component skills improving gradually, but the overall task requiring all of them to work together. Then the task performance might look like a sudden jump, even though none of the underlying changes was sudden. We should distinguish that from a model actually discovering a new way of computing something.

And then I’d like to see interventions. If we think a particular component is necessary, can we disrupt it and make the capability disappear? If we train that component explicitly, does the broader capability appear earlier? That would give us a much stronger explanation than simply looking at a performance curve and saying, “Well, something emerged here.”

r001.rationale: The response proposes measuring component skills as training increases, but does not specifically propose evaluating earlier training checkpoints to determine when those skills first appear.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see us move beyond looking at a single aggregate performance score and ask what the network has actually learned to do. A task may require several capabilities, and if any one of them is missing, the whole task fails. So a sudden jump in task performance doesn’t necessarily mean that all of those capabilities appeared suddenly. They may have been developing gradually.

We could design controlled tasks where we know which components are required, test those components separately as training proceeds, and then study how the network combines them. And we should do interventions—disable a component or provide an intermediate result—to check whether our explanation is causal. That would help distinguish a genuinely new capability from a threshold effect in how we measure performance.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing component capabilities separately as training proceeds and asks whether they developed gradually or appeared suddenly, which communicates tracking when they emerge across training.
